1

Summary: evidence and conclusions

VerdictNO-GORisk tier 3 of 3

The shop cannot be delivered as it is. Under the expected midnight rush it sells far more pairs than it has and charges people twice, anyone can read customers' addresses or wipe all orders, one bad request or a restart takes the sale down and loses paid orders, and it is not connected to a real payment provider.

If it were delivered or launched now

Within the first minute, hundreds of customers would be charged for sneakers that do not exist and many would be charged twice, while the page took several seconds to load. Anyone could download every buyer's email and home address, buy at a price they choose, or delete all orders with one request; a single malformed request would stop the sale for everyone, and the restart would erase every paid order. The client would face refunds, chargebacks, a personal-data breach to report, and angry customers on launch night.

The three questions

These answers measure how complete the testing and the inspection are, not whether the app is ready: the verdict says that.

QuestionAnswerEvidence
1. Is the test harness properly set up?No0 of 13 harness checks met; of the 7 kinds of problem that came back, 4 have no automatic test that would catch them and 3 are only partly caught.
2. Are the performance tests comprehensive?Partly6 of 8 kinds of performance test run; 1 passed, 5 failed.
3. Does the architecture review cover hidden problems?Yes9 of 9 places examined; 18 hidden problems found.
  • The test harness is not set up: 12 of 13 checks are not met and 1 could not be verified, and of the 7 kinds of problem that came back, 4 have no automatic test that would catch them and 3 are only partly caught. Expect the same bugs to return after the next change.
  • The performance tests are not fully comprehensive: 2 of 8 kinds this product needs were not run (long run, on a production-like setup). 5 of the 6 that were run failed (see each).
  • The review looked in all 9 places where hidden problems usually sit. It found 18 problems there.

Before delivery: 8 blockers

  1. Make the purchase safe: the price comes from the server, stock is reserved atomically before charging, one pair per customer is enforced in the database, every purchase carries one idempotency key, a time-out leaves the order pending, and a job settles and reconciles payments.
  2. Close access: a real sign-in with signed sessions, an ownership check on every order, admin routes removed or behind an admin role, and the search route fixed or removed.
  3. Rotate the payment key that is written in the code, move it to a secret setting and remove it from the history.
  4. Keep orders safe across crashes and deploys: a persistent database with backups and migrations, no deletion at start-up, error handling that answers 400 instead of crashing, and a graceful shutdown.
  5. Connect the real payment provider and try a purchase, a decline and a refund in its test mode, then one small live purchase and refund.
  6. Add the sale opening time (date, time and time zone) and a pause switch on the server.
  7. Make the page hold the expected crowd and keep bots out: one query per page view with a short cache, a waiting room or busy page, and limits on sign-ins and purchases; then pass the load and race tests on a staging copy.
  8. Prepare to run the sale: health checks, error tracking and alerts to a named person, clean logs, backups and a rollback that have been tried, and a rehearsed launch runbook.

Who does each, how big it is, and the conditions: Recommendations.

When it could be delivered Estimate only: about three to four weeks of developer work for the blockers, plus a staging copy and a re-inspection, so delivery is realistic no earlier than late November 2026 if work starts now.

How to read the results

Yes, Partly, No
Counted by software from the record: everything done is Yes, at least half is Partly, less than half is No.
Blocker
Delivery can't happen until it's done.
Condition
Also required, at the time shown, but not a reason to stop on its own.
Cannot verify
The inspector didn't have what was needed to check it. It is not a pass: each one says what's needed.
Codes
Codes like ARC-11 are problems found (see What to fix). Codes like A-09 are checklist items, under "Full checklist" in each evidence section.
Evidence A, B, C
A: the inspector ran or measured it. B: the inspector read the code or settings. C: someone's statement, which never counts as proof.
Dotted underline
Hover over it, or tap it, for an explanation.

Results: the three questions

1

Is the test harness properly set up?

No

The tests, automatic checks and AI-agent instructions that stop the next change, by a person or an AI agent, from breaking something or bringing an old bug back.

Evidence

0 of 13 harness checks met.

In place

None.

Missing or unproven
  • H-01 Agent instructions exist Does not meet
    Found: No AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or equivalent in the repository.
  • H-02 Agent instructions are true Does not meet
    Found: There is no instruction file whose commands could be checked. (The README commands were run and work; see R-02.)
  • H-03 Agents know the rules and boundaries Does not meet
    Found: No file tells agents the rules that must never be broken (stock, one per customer, server-side price, never delete orders at start-up).
  • H-04 Lessons are recorded for agents Does not meet
    Found: None of the recurring problems from the pilot is recorded as a rule for agents.
  • H-05 Agent instructions are lean and safe Does not meet
    Found: No instruction file exists to be lean and safe.
  • H-06 Every promise has a test Does not meet
    Found: Every Must criterion except AC-07 has a test in acceptance/tests/flash-sale.spec.mjs; AC-07 (never oversell) relies on a race test that is not in the repository. Rules without a test: one per customer across separate purchases, orders survive a restart, admin routes closed.
  • H-07 Tests check outcomes Does not meet
    Found: Most tests count orders, amounts and charges (good), but none checks what should disappear: AC-02 passed while the sign-in box stayed on screen (evidence/acceptance/AC-02-test-finished-1.png).
  • H-08 Failure paths are tested Does not meet
    Found: Tests cover tampering (AC-03), another user's data (AC-06), double submission (AC-04), a stuck provider (AC-08) and a missing address (AC-11); none covers malformed requests, restarts or admin access.
  • H-09 Tests are reliable Does not meet
    Found: Three runs with retries off: the same 7 tests failed in every run (21 failures, 15 passes, no flaky results) (logs/acceptance-run.txt).
  • H-10 Every change goes through CI Does not meet
    Found: No CI configuration in the repository; the delivered commit fails its own tests.
  • H-11 Lint and type checks pass Does not meet
    Found: No linter, formatter or type checker is configured (no ESLint, Prettier or TypeScript configuration, no check script).
  • H-12 Security checks are automated Does not meet
    Found: No secret scanning or dependency scanning in CI or in commit hooks.
  • H-13 Changes get an independent review Cannot verify
    Needed to verify: The pull-request history with reviews from the code host. The repository holds a single commit by "Shop team" with no merge commits, which suggests no review step, but reviews would live on the code host, which was not shared.

Conclusion

The test harness is not set up: 12 of 13 checks are not met and 1 could not be verified, and of the 7 kinds of problem that came back, 4 have no automatic test that would catch them and 3 are only partly caught. Expect the same bugs to return after the next change.

Recommendation

Most needed first:

  1. Add integration tests. Would catch: Customers charged twice for one purchase; More sold than in stock, and more than one pair per customer; Customers charged but no order recorded; The server trusts the browser: someone else's data, the price, admin functions; Errors crash the site or show the code to visitors; Slow pages and long waits under load or with a slow payment provider.
    Integration tests catch parts that work alone but not together: database rules and transactions, a stand-in payment provider that is slow or fails. Skills and tools: test-driven-development.
  2. Add load and race tests. Would catch: Customers charged twice for one purchase; More sold than in stock, and more than one pair per customer; Customers charged but no order recorded; Slow pages and long waits under load or with a slow payment provider.
    Load and race tests catch slow pages, overselling and double charges when many people arrive at once. Skills and tools: peak-traffic-test.
  3. Add automatic scans. Would catch: More sold than in stock, and more than one pair per customer; The server trusts the browser: someone else's data, the price, admin functions; Errors crash the site or show the code to visitors.
    Automatic scans catch leaked keys, risky code patterns, libraries with known security holes. Skills and tools: launch-review.
  4. Run the end-to-end tests in a browser on every change (CI), and extend them. Would catch: Customers charged twice for one purchase; The server trusts the browser: someone else's data, the price, admin functions; Sign-in box does not go away after signing in.
    End-to-end tests in a browser catch a user journey that breaks: signing in, buying, seeing the order. Skills and tools: acceptance-test, webapp-testing.
  5. Add unit tests. Would catch: Errors crash the site or show the code to visitors.
    Unit tests catch a rule or calculation that is wrong: prices, limits, reading input, dates. Skills and tools: test-driven-development.
  6. Add visual tests. Would catch: Sign-in box does not go away after signing in.
    Visual tests catch a screen that looks wrong although it works: something that should disappear stays, things overlap, a layout breaks on a phone. Skills and tools: acceptance-test, webapp-testing, Playwright screenshot comparison.
  7. Add self-checks. Would catch: Customers charged but no order recorded.
    Self-checks catch the app checking itself: refusing to start with missing or unsafe settings, a health check that tests what matters, a quick test after every deploy. Skills and tools: verification-before-completion.

Are the performance tests comprehensive?

Partly

Whether every kind of performance test this product needs was run. Whether the app passed each one is shown beside it.

Evidence

Kind of testResultWhat it showed
Load at the target and above itFailedStepped test at 50%, 100%, 150% and 200% of 600 requests per second: the product page missed its 500 ms budget from the first step (95th percentile 2.38 s) and served at most about 237 views per second. (run by the reviewer)
Repeated runs, all keptFailedThe full plan ran twice and both runs are kept; both failed the same way (2.38 s and 2.35 s at 50% of the target), so the failure is not luck. (run by the reviewer)
Rush on something limitedFailedRace test run twice: 1,957 and 1,956 orders confirmed for 100 pairs; 957 and 956 buyers charged twice. (run by the reviewer)
Slow or failing partnerFailedPayments at 3 to 10 s: 400 charges for 400 clicks by 200 buyers. Payments stuck for 30 s: the shopper waited 30 s and got an error page. (run by the reviewer)
Beyond capacityFailedAt 150% and 200% of the target nobody was turned away politely (no 429 or 503); everyone waited up to 8 s and thousands of page views were never served. The app did not crash and recovered after the test. (run by the reviewer)
Long runNot runNot run: an hour at normal traffic means little until the capacity and data-loss blockers are fixed. Memory grew from 66 MB to 201 MB in one two-minute run, so this test should be run after the fixes. (run by the reviewer)
Page speed on phonesPassedLighthouse mobile on the local copy: score 98, Largest Contentful Paint 1.6 s, layout shift 0.085, no blocking time. (run by the reviewer)
On a production-like setupNot runNot run: there is no staging copy and no hosting has been chosen; all numbers come from one laptop-sized machine with simulated payments and database delay. (run by the reviewer)

Conclusion

The performance tests are not fully comprehensive: 2 of 8 kinds this product needs were not run (long run, on a production-like setup). 5 of the 6 that were run failed (see each).

Recommendation

Run these tests:

  • Long run. An hour or more at normal traffic without slowing down, filling up or running out of memory.
  • On a production-like setup. The numbers hold on the real hosting, with a realistic amount of data, not only on a laptop.

Skills: peak-traffic-test runs the load, beyond-capacity, rush and slow-partner tests; Lighthouse measures page speed on phones.

  • ARC-03 Critical Customers set their own price

  • ARC-12 High No real payment provider is connected or tested
  • OPS-02 High A deploy or restart cuts off purchases in progress
  • PERF-01 High The sale page slows to 2 to 8 seconds at half the expected crowd
  • ARC-08 High Nothing stops people buying before midnight, and the sale cannot be paused
  • ARC-10 Medium Settings are written in the code or ignored, and the app starts with wrong ones
  • ARC-09 Medium Orders can be paid without a shipping address
  • SEC-06 Medium Error pages show the code's internals
  • PERF-03 Medium No limits on request size or waiting time
  • PERF-02 Medium Past its limit the site makes everyone wait instead of turning some people away politely
  • ARC-11 Medium The confirmation email is sent while the shopper waits

Conclusion

The review looked in all 9 places where hidden problems usually sit. It found 18 problems there.

Recommendation

Fix the hidden problems (see What to fix), and for each add the test that would have caught it, so it can't come back unnoticed.

Decisions only the owner can make

  • Choose the payment provider, the email provider and the hosting (with a staging copy). details: ARC-12 R-06
  • Set the sale date, the time zone of "midnight", and whether a virtual waiting room (a paid service) is worth it for a 100-pair drop. details: ARC-08 PERF-02
  • Agree how much order data may be lost and how quickly the shop must be back after an outage. details: R-07
  • Decide how long customers' email and home addresses are kept after the sale. details: D-11
  • Confirm whether AI coding assistants are used on this code; if not, the agent-instruction checks no longer apply. details: HAR-01

What customers would notice today

  • Paying for sneakers that never arrive, because more pairs were sold than exist.
  • Two charges for one pair after a double-click or a reload.
  • A sale page that takes 2 to 8 seconds to load at midnight, or shows "We are very busy".
  • A Buy button that spins for half a minute and then shows technical text.
  • The whole site going down, and paid orders disappearing after it comes back.
  • Their email and home address visible to strangers.
  • The sign-in box still on screen after signing in.

What to fix: every open problem

31 open problems, blockers first, then by severity.

  • SEC-01CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Anyone can read any customer's order, including their home address

    Impact
    Anyone can collect every buyer's email address and home address by trying order numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:120-124 (GET /api/orders/:id): no sign-in or ownership check. Evidence: With no token, curl -s localhost:3310/api/orders/1 returned Alice's email, address and amount with HTTP 200 (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 1). Acceptance test AC-06 failed in all three runs: Bob and a logged-out visitor both got HTTP 200. Tickets: #8.
    Evidence
    With no token, curl -s localhost:3310/api/orders/1 returned Alice's email, address and amount with HTTP 200 (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 1). Acceptance test AC-06 failed in all three runs: Bob and a logged-out visitor both got HTTP 200.
    Fix
    Require a signed-in customer and look the order up by id and customer together (WHERE id = ? AND customer = ?); answer 404 otherwise.
    Done when
    AC-06 passes three runs in a row, and the request in evidence/probes-access.txt step 1 answers 401 or 404.
  • SEC-02CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Anyone can act as any customer: the sign-in "token" is just the email address, unsigned

    Impact
    Anyone who knows or guesses a customer's email address can see their orders and address, or buy in their name. There is no password, email link or code.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:79-83 (POST /api/login returns base64 of whatever email it is given) and app/server.mjs:42-47 (currentUser decodes the token without checking a signature); TOKEN_SECRET (run.mjs:21) is never read. Evidence: A token made by hand (printf '{"email":"alice@example.test"}' | base64), without signing in, returned Alice's orders from GET /api/my-orders (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 2). Semgrep unverified-token-decode at app/server.mjs:46.
    Evidence
    A token made by hand (printf '{"email":"alice@example.test"}' | base64), without signing in, returned Alice's orders from GET /api/my-orders (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 2). Semgrep unverified-token-decode at app/server.mjs:46.
    Fix
    Use a proven sign-in method (an email link or one-time code from an auth provider, or a hosted auth service) and signed, expiring session tokens whose secret comes from the environment; verify the token on every request.
    Done when
    A hand-made or edited token gets 401 from /api/my-orders and /api/buy, and an automated test proves it.
  • SEC-03CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Admin functions are open to everyone: one request deletes every order

    Impact
    Anyone on the internet can delete all orders and set the stock to any number in the middle of the sale, and anyone can read the sales figures.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:132-137 (POST /api/admin/reset) and app/server.mjs:139-150 (GET /api/admin/stats) check nothing; the x-admin-token header the tests send is ignored and ADMIN_TOKEN (run.mjs:22) is never read. Evidence: Without any token, POST /api/admin/reset answered {"ok":true} and Alice's orders went from 3 to none; GET /api/admin/stats answered HTTP 200 with sales and payment totals (evidence/probes-access.txt, steps 7 and 10). Tickets: #16.
    Evidence
    Without any token, POST /api/admin/reset answered {"ok":true} and Alice's orders went from 3 to none; GET /api/admin/stats answered HTTP 200 with sales and payment totals (evidence/probes-access.txt, steps 7 and 10).
    Fix
    Remove the reset route from anything that faces the internet (test builds only, behind a setting production refuses); put the stats behind an admin role with personal accounts.
    Done when
    Both routes answer 401 or 404 without an admin session, checked by an automated test that calls them with no credentials.
  • SEC-04CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    The search address hands out every customer's email and address (SQL injection)

    Impact
    One crafted search returns every buyer's email and home address, and the same hole could change or delete data.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:96-100 (GET /api/search): the search text is pasted into the SQL statement. The page never uses this route.. Evidence: q=zzz' UNION SELECT id, customer || ' / ' || address, amount_cents FROM orders -- returned every order's email and address (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 8). Semgrep sql-built-from-strings-js at app/server.mjs:98.
    Evidence
    q=zzz' UNION SELECT id, customer || ' / ' || address, amount_cents FROM orders -- returned every order's email and address (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 8). Semgrep sql-built-from-strings-js at app/server.mjs:98.
    Fix
    Delete the unused route, or pass the search text as a parameter (WHERE name LIKE ?).
    Done when
    The request in step 8 returns an empty list or 400, and Semgrep sql-built-from-strings-js no longer fires on line 98.
  • SEC-05CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    A payment key named like a live key is written in the code and in the git history

    Impact
    Anyone who gets a copy of the code (contractors, the client's staff, a leaked backup) could charge or refund through the shop's payment account. Every copy of the app uses the same key.
    Who
    Developer, with whoever owns the payment provider account
    Where
    app/server.mjs:10 (PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY = 'pay_…', redacted), committed in bb6c41e; the PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY setting in run.mjs:20 is ignored. Evidence: Gitleaks rule generic-api-key fired on app/server.mjs:10 in the current files and in the git history (scans/gitleaks-files.json, scans/gitleaks-history.json).
    Evidence
    Gitleaks rule generic-api-key fired on app/server.mjs:10 in the current files and in the git history (scans/gitleaks-files.json, scans/gitleaks-history.json).
    Fix
    Rotate the key at the payment provider now. Read it from a secret setting, refuse to start without it, keep test and live keys apart, and remove it from the history before the repository is handed over.
    Done when
    The old key is revoked at the provider, Gitleaks finds nothing in the files, and the app refuses to start without PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY.
  • ARC-01CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    It sells far more pairs than exist when many people buy at once

    Impact
    In the race test, 1,957 purchases were confirmed and charged for 100 pairs: 1,857 customers would pay for sneakers that do not exist.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:107-111: reads the stock, charges the card, then writes stock = <the number read earlier> - 1; nothing in the database stops the stock going below zero. Evidence: Race test, two runs: 1,957 and 1,956 orders for 100 pairs, stock counter left at 93 (peak-traffic/oversell1/oversell-summary.md, peak-traffic/oversell2/oversell-summary.md). Load run 1 ended with 2,939 paid orders for 100 pairs (peak-traffic/run1/stats-after.txt). Semgrep stock-lost-update-sql at line 111. Tickets: #4.
    Evidence
    Race test, two runs: 1,957 and 1,956 orders for 100 pairs, stock counter left at 93 (peak-traffic/oversell1/oversell-summary.md, peak-traffic/oversell2/oversell-summary.md). Load run 1 ended with 2,939 paid orders for 100 pairs (peak-traffic/run1/stats-after.txt). Semgrep stock-lost-update-sql at line 111.
    Fix
    Reserve first with one atomic update (UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0, and check that one row changed), then charge, then confirm; give the pair back only when the payment definitely failed; add CHECK (stock >= 0).
    Done when
    The race test with the same plan shows at most 100 sold, and sold + awaiting payment + remaining = 100.
  • ARC-02CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    One pair per customer is not enforced: double clicks and repeat purchases charge again

    Impact
    A shopper who double-clicks, reloads or presses Buy again pays again for another pair, and one person can buy as many pairs as they like.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:102-118 (no check for an existing order, no unique rule on orders) and app/server.mjs:49-57 (no idempotency key sent to the payment provider). Evidence: Two clicks at the same moment gave Dave 2 orders and 2 charges; Alice bought 3 pairs (evidence/probes-access.txt, steps 5 and 6). AC-04 failed in all three runs (2 orders after a double-click). Race test: 957 buyers charged twice (peak-traffic/oversell1). Tickets: #1, #2, #3.
    Evidence
    Two clicks at the same moment gave Dave 2 orders and 2 charges; Alice bought 3 pairs (evidence/probes-access.txt, steps 5 and 6). AC-04 failed in all three runs (2 orders after a double-click). Race test: 957 buyers charged twice (peak-traffic/oversell1).
    Fix
    Enforce one live order per customer and product in the database (a unique index). Give each purchase attempt an id from the page, reuse it on retries, store it with the order and pass it to the provider as Idempotency-Key; answer a repeat with the existing order.
    Done when
    AC-04 passes three runs in a row, and the race test shows no buyer charged twice.
  • ARC-03CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Customers set their own price

    Impact
    Anyone can buy the $49.99 sneakers for one cent by editing the request.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:105, :110, :114: the price sent by the browser is charged and stored; the page sends it at shared/public/app.js:121. Evidence: Bob's purchase with "price":1 was confirmed as amountCents: 1 and the provider charged one cent (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 3; provider total 29,995 cents = 6 × 4,999 + 1). AC-03 failed in all three runs. Semgrep price-from-client at line 105. Tickets: #9.
    Evidence
    Bob's purchase with "price":1 was confirmed as amountCents: 1 and the provider charged one cent (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 3; provider total 29,995 cents = 6 × 4,999 + 1). AC-03 failed in all three runs. Semgrep price-from-client at line 105.
    Fix
    Take the price from the product record on the server and ignore any price from the browser (or refuse a request whose price differs).
    Done when
    AC-03 passes three runs in a row.
  • ARC-04CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    A crash or deploy during payment leaves customers charged with no order

    Impact
    Customers pay and get nothing, and the shop has no record that they paid; it finds out only when they complain.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:110-115: the card is charged first, and only then are the stock and the order written; nothing records the attempt before the charge, and nothing compares the provider's charges with the orders. Evidence: With the payment provider running on its own and answering in 3 seconds, one malformed request (a crash) and a SIGTERM (a deploy), each sent 1 second into a purchase: the provider recorded the charge and the app had no order (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt, parts D and E). Tickets: #7, #10.
    Evidence
    With the payment provider running on its own and answering in 3 seconds, one malformed request (a crash) and a SIGTERM (a deploy), each sent 1 second into a purchase: the provider recorded the charge and the app had no order (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt, parts D and E).
    Fix
    Record a pending order (with the reserved pair and the idempotency key) before charging, and mark it paid or failed afterwards. A background job settles pending orders with the provider and compares the provider's charges with the orders, raising an alert on any difference.
    Done when
    Both reproductions end with a paid or refunded order for every provider charge, and a reconciliation run reports no differences.
  • ARC-05CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Every restart deletes all orders and puts the 100 pairs back on sale

    Impact
    A crash, a deploy or a host restart during the sale erases every paid order (who bought and where to ship) and lets another 100 pairs be sold.
    Who
    Developer, with the hosting provider
    Where
    app/server.mjs:13 (openDb() opens an in-memory database) and app/server.mjs:14-27 (CREATE TABLE and seed(), which runs DELETE FROM orders, on every start). Evidence: One paid order before a restart, none after it, and the stock back at 100 (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, part C). Tickets: #7.
    Evidence
    One paid order before a restart, none after it, and the stock back at 100 (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, part C).
    Fix
    Use a persistent database (managed Postgres, or a SQLite file on a persistent disk) with automatic backups; create tables through versioned migrations; seed demo data only in tests and never delete data at start-up.
    Done when
    An order placed before a restart is still there after it, start-up code contains no DELETE, and a backup has been restored once.
  • ARC-06CriticalBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    One malformed request takes the whole site down

    Impact
    Anyone, or one buggy browser, can stop the sale for everyone with a single request, as often as they like.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:34-40 (JSON.parse inside the request's end callback, outside any error handling) and app/server.mjs:166 (the address is parsed from the Host header outside the error handling); run.mjs:38-43 then stops the payment provider too, and nothing restarts either. Evidence: A body of {not json sent to /api/login, and a request with Host: bad host, each made the server exit with code 1; the site stopped answering (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, parts A and B). Semgrep json-parse-in-stream-callback (line 38) and url-parse-outside-try (line 166). Tickets: #5, #6.
    Evidence
    A body of {not json sent to /api/login, and a request with Host: bad host, each made the server exit with code 1; the site stopped answering (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, parts A and B). Semgrep json-parse-in-stream-callback (line 38) and url-parse-outside-try (line 166).
    Fix
    Parse bodies inside error handling and answer 400; build the URL inside the error handling (or answer 400 on a bad Host); limit body size; run the app under a supervisor that restarts it.
    Done when
    Both requests get 400 and the site keeps answering, checked by an automated test.
  • SEC-08HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Nothing slows down scripts: bots can sign in and buy as fast as they like

    Impact
    In a sneaker drop, scripts buy faster than people. With no limits and no bot protection, resellers can take the stock before real customers finish loading the page.
    Who
    Developer, with the hosting provider for edge protection
    Where
    app/server.mjs:79-118: no rate limit or bot check on POST /api/login or POST /api/buy. Evidence: 60 sign-ins in a row from one address all answered 200 (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 12); 1,000 scripted buyers placed 1,957 orders in the race test (peak-traffic/oversell1/oversell-summary.md).
    Evidence
    60 sign-ins in a row from one address all answered 200 (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 12); 1,000 scripted buyers placed 1,957 orders in the race test (peak-traffic/oversell1/oversell-summary.md).
    Fix
    Limit sign-ins and purchases per account and per address in a shared store, and put bot protection or a virtual waiting room in front of the sale.
    Done when
    The 60-request burst gets 429 after the limit, and a waiting room or bot check sits in front of checkout during the sale.
  • ARC-07HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    When the payment provider is slow, shoppers wait up to 30 seconds and then get an error

    Impact
    When the provider slows down at midnight, the Buy button spins for up to 30 seconds and then shows technical text; shoppers try again and may pay twice. There is no "we are confirming your payment" state.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:49-57: the call to the provider has no time limit and no idempotency key, and any answer other than success becomes a 500 error. Evidence: Provider stuck for 30 s: the shopper got HTTP 500 with a stack trace after 30.0 s (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt, part G). Provider at 8 s: the purchase took 8.3 s (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, part F). AC-08 failed in all three runs (page stuck on "Placing your order…"). Slow-partner race test (3 to 10 s per charge): 400 charges for 400 clicks by 200 buyers (peak-traffic/slow-partner/). Semgrep fetch-without-timeout at lines 50, 135, 142. Tickets: #12.
    Evidence
    Provider stuck for 30 s: the shopper got HTTP 500 with a stack trace after 30.0 s (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt, part G). Provider at 8 s: the purchase took 8.3 s (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, part F). AC-08 failed in all three runs (page stuck on "Placing your order…"). Slow-partner race test (3 to 10 s per charge): 400 charges for 400 clicks by 200 buyers (peak-traffic/slow-partner/). Semgrep fetch-without-timeout at lines 50, 135, 142.
    Fix
    Give the call a time limit (2 to 5 seconds). On a time-out keep the order pending (not failed), answer "we are confirming your payment", settle it with the provider's lookup or webhook, and reuse one idempotency key per purchase attempt.
    Done when
    AC-08 passes three runs in a row, and the slow-partner test shows provider charges equal to paid orders with no buyer charged twice.
  • ARC-08HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Nothing stops people buying before midnight, and the sale cannot be paused

    Impact
    Anyone who finds the page before midnight (resellers watch for it) can buy the stock before the email goes out. If something goes wrong during the sale, the only way to stop it is to shut the site down, which today deletes every order.
    Who
    Developer, with the product owner for the date and time zone
    Where
    app/server.mjs has no opening time, no pause switch and no /api/admin/sale route; the page's opening-time logic (shared/public/app.js:44-60) waits for a sale field the server never sends. Evidence: AC-12 and AC-13 failed in all three runs at their first step: POST /api/admin/sale answered 404; GET /api/products/1 has no sale field; purchases succeed at any time (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 11).
    Evidence
    AC-12 and AC-13 failed in all three runs at their first step: POST /api/admin/sale answered 404; GET /api/products/1 has no sale field; purchases succeed at any time (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 11).
    Fix
    Add a sale window on the server: the opening time as a full date, time and time zone from one setting, logged at start-up and sent to the page, and a pause switch that needs no deploy. POST /api/buy refuses (403) before opening and while paused.
    Done when
    AC-12 and AC-13 pass three runs in a row.
  • ARC-12HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    No real payment provider is connected or tested

    Impact
    As delivered, the shop cannot take real money, and the real provider's behaviour (declines, card checks, refunds, limits, notifications) has never been tried.
    Who
    Developer, with the product owner (choice of provider)
    Where
    app/server.mjs:49-57 calls only the local simulator's /charge; the README says payments and email are simulators. Evidence: The code and the README; no provider library, webhook route or refund path exists.
    Evidence
    The code and the README; no provider library, webhook route or refund path exists.
    Fix
    Choose the provider, connect its hosted checkout or payment API with amounts set on the server and idempotency keys, verify its notifications, and try a purchase, a decline and a refund in its test mode, then one small real purchase and refund before launch.

  • PERF-01HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    The sale page slows to 2 to 8 seconds at half the expected crowd

    Impact
    At midnight shoppers wait 2 to 8 seconds for the page, and the server manages only about half of the page views it is asked for, so many people see "We are very busy. Retrying…".
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:85-94 (GET /api/products/:id: one query for the product, one for the reviews, then one per review author, so 14 per page view), no caching, and a pool of 10 database connections that waits forever. Evidence: Two load runs (peak-traffic/run1/load-summary.md, peak-traffic/run2/load-summary.md): product page 95th percentile 2.38 s and 2.35 s at 50% of the target (budget 500 ms), 5.07 to 5.20 s at 100%, 7.69 to 8.14 s at 200%; it served 205 to 237 page views per second against a target of 450. Semgrep db-query-in-loop-js at line 90. Tickets: #11.
    Evidence
    Two load runs (peak-traffic/run1/load-summary.md, peak-traffic/run2/load-summary.md): product page 95th percentile 2.38 s and 2.35 s at 50% of the target (budget 500 ms), 5.07 to 5.20 s at 100%, 7.69 to 8.14 s at 200%; it served 205 to 237 page views per second against a target of 450. Semgrep db-query-in-loop-js at line 90.
    Fix
    Read the reviews with their authors in one query (a JOIN); cache the product answer for 1 to 2 seconds (the stock on the page may lag; the purchase stays exact); serve the page files from a CDN.
    Done when
    The same load plan passes at 100% and 150% of the target (product page under 500 ms for 95% of requests, under 1% errors).
  • OPS-01HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    Nobody would notice problems: no health check, monitoring or alerts, and the logs hold customers' email addresses

    Impact
    During the sale, crashes, slow pages and payment failures would be discovered by customers, not by the team, and the logs would hold personal data.
    Who
    Developer, with the hosting provider
    Where
    No health route (GET /health answers 404), no error tracking, metrics or alerts anywhere in the repository; app/server.mjs:62 logs customer email addresses; app/server.mjs:172 logs raw errors; no request id. Evidence: GET /health answered 404 (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 11); no monitoring or alerting code or configuration in the 15 files of commit bb6c41e.
    Evidence
    GET /health answered 404 (evidence/probes-access.txt, step 11); no monitoring or alerting code or configuration in the 15 files of commit bb6c41e.
    Fix
    Add a liveness check and a readiness check (database and payment provider), error tracking, dashboards for requests, errors and response times, and alerts that reach a named on-call person; write structured logs with a request id and no personal data.
    Done when
    A test alert reaches the on-call person, both health checks answer, and a log line from a purchase carries a request id and no email address.
  • OPS-02HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    A deploy or restart cuts off purchases in progress

    Impact
    Every deploy during the sale cuts off shoppers who are paying: they are charged, get no answer and have no order (see ARC-04).
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs does not handle SIGTERM (no server.close()), and run.mjs:35-37 passes SIGTERM straight on. Evidence: SIGTERM sent 1 second into a 3-second payment: the app exited at once (code 143), the shopper got no answer, the provider recorded the charge and no order existed (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt, part E).
    Evidence
    SIGTERM sent 1 second into a 3-second payment: the app exited at once (code 143), the shopper got no answer, the provider recorded the charge and no order existed (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt, part E).
    Fix
    On SIGTERM stop taking new requests, finish those in progress (allowing longer than the payment time limit), then exit; deploy one instance at a time behind a health check.
    Done when
    A restart under load drops no requests, and every provider charge has an order.
  • OPS-03HighBlocks launchOpen · Confirmed

    No backups, rollback plan, runbook or launch-day plan

    Impact
    If anything goes wrong at midnight nobody knows what to do, and there is nothing to restore the orders from.
    Who
    Developer, with the hosting provider and the product owner
    Where
    The repository and the hand-over: no hosting chosen, no deploy or rollback configuration, no backups (the database lives in memory), no runbook. Evidence: The 15 files of commit bb6c41e and the README: none covers deploys, backups, rollback or incidents.
    Evidence
    The 15 files of commit bb6c41e and the README: none covers deploys, backups, rollback or incidents.

  • ARC-10MediumCondition: Before deliveryOpen · Confirmed

    Settings are written in the code or ignored, and the app starts with wrong ones

    Impact
    The team may believe it can switch off test routes and demo data and set secrets for production; none of those switches exist. A wrong payment address is noticed only when the first customer pays.
    Who
    Developer
    Where
    app/server.mjs:8-10 reads only PORT and PAYMENT_URL; run.mjs:17-25 also sets PAYMENT_SECRET_KEY, TOKEN_SECRET, ADMIN_TOKEN, DEMO_LOGIN, ENABLE_TEST_ROUTES and SEED_DEMO_DATA, which the app never reads. The README says the app reads its other settings from the environment.. Evidence: Started with PAYMENT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1: the server started normally and the first purchase failed with HTTP 500 "fetch failed" (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, part I). A search for process.env in the code (system map).
    Evidence
    Started with PAYMENT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1: the server started normally and the first purchase failed with HTTP 500 "fetch failed" (evidence/probes-restarts.txt, part I). A search for process.env in the code (system map).

Performance

Will it hold the expected traffic and stay correct?

The sale page manages about half the expected opening crowd, and the rush breaks the stock and one-per-customer rules. Page speed for a single phone visitor is good.

Kinds of performance test

Kind of testWhat it provesRun byResultWhat it showed
Load at the target and above itIt holds the expected traffic, and shows where it breaks.reviewerFailedStepped test at 50%, 100%, 150% and 200% of 600 requests per second: the product page missed its 500 ms budget from the first step (95th percentile 2.38 s) and served at most about 237 views per second.
Repeated runs, all keptThe same test run at least twice gives the same answer, and failed runs are kept too. Its result says whether the runs agreed.reviewerFailedThe full plan ran twice and both runs are kept; both failed the same way (2.38 s and 2.35 s at 50% of the target), so the failure is not luck.
Rush on something limitedMany people buying or booking the last items at the same moment never oversell or pay twice.reviewerFailedRace test run twice: 1,957 and 1,956 orders confirmed for 100 pairs; 957 and 956 buyers charged twice.
Slow or failing partnerWhen payment, email or an AI service is slow or down, nobody is charged twice or left stuck.reviewerFailedPayments at 3 to 10 s: 400 charges for 400 clicks by 200 buyers. Payments stuck for 30 s: the shopper waited 30 s and got an error page.
Beyond capacityPast its limit it turns people away politely and recovers, instead of crashing.reviewerFailedAt 150% and 200% of the target nobody was turned away politely (no 429 or 503); everyone waited up to 8 s and thousands of page views were never served. The app did not crash and recovered after the test.
Long runAn hour or more at normal traffic without slowing down, filling up or running out of memory.reviewerNot runNot run: an hour at normal traffic means little until the capacity and data-loss blockers are fixed. Memory grew from 66 MB to 201 MB in one two-minute run, so this test should be run after the fixes.
Page speed on phonesPeople on mid-range phones get the page quickly.reviewerPassedLighthouse mobile on the local copy: score 98, Largest Contentful Paint 1.6 s, layout shift 0.085, no blocking time.
On a production-like setupThe numbers hold on the real hosting, with a realistic amount of data, not only on a laptop.reviewerNot runNot run: there is no staging copy and no hosting has been chosen; all numbers come from one laptop-sized machine with simulated payments and database delay.

Target 600 requests per second at the peak: 450 product-page views (95% under 500 ms) and 150 purchases (95% under 1,500 ms), from the owner's brief (3,000 visitors in 60 s, peak factor 3).

Tested on The reviewer's local copy on one 4-core cloud container, with k6 on the same machine (machine on average about a quarter busy during the runs, so the load generator was not the limit). Simulated database (pool of 10, 3 ms per query) and payment provider (80 to 200 ms, 2% of calls stuck for 30 s). Not production-like: no staging exists.

Race test

1,000 buyers each clicked Buy twice at the same moment for 100 pairs. Every click was either accepted or failed; none was refused as sold out or already ordered.

MeasureValue
Clicks sent2,000
Purchases confirmed1,957
Server errors or time-outs43
Refused (sold out, already ordered)0
Buyers charged twice957
Orders in the database1,957
Stock counter afterwards93

Slow partner

With the provider taking 3 to 10 seconds per charge, 200 buyers clicking twice produced 400 charges and 400 orders for 100 pairs, and the stock counter ended at 99. With the provider stuck, a shopper waited 30 seconds and got an error page; in the acceptance test the page stayed on "Placing your order…".

Not ready for the expected crowd: the sale page slows to 2 to 8 seconds from half the expected traffic, and under a rush the shop confirms and charges far more orders than it has pairs. The purchase steps "pass" at 150% and 200% only because the stock counter had reached zero, so most purchases were quick "sold out" answers. Note: the purchase speed at the higher steps is not meaningful for the same reason.

8

Architecture

Is the structure sound for the agreed requirements?

One Node.js process serves the page and a small JSON API from an in-memory SQLite database (wrapped to behave like a hosted database with a pool of 10 connections). A purchase reads the stock, charges the card through the payment provider, writes the stock and the order, and sends an email, all inside the request. The payment provider and email are simulators. (Reviewer-built: the author handed in no architecture; full map in 01-system-map.md.)

The design keeps everything in one process's memory and does the whole purchase (check, charge, write, email) inside one request, with the card charged first. That is why it oversells, double-charges and loses paid orders on any restart.

flowchart LR
  B[Shopper browser] --> R[Router: no auth layer]
  X[Anyone] --> R
  R --> L[/api/login: unsigned token/]
  R --> P[/api/products, /api/search/]
  R --> BUY[/api/buy: check, charge, write/]
  R --> O[/api/orders/:id, /api/my-orders/]
  R --> ADM[/api/admin/reset, /stats: no check/]
  P --> DB[(SQLite in memory)]
  BUY --> DB
  O --> DB
  ADM --> DB
  BUY -- no time limit --> PAY[(Payment provider)]
  BUY --> MAIL[Email, in the request]

Security

Who can do what, and can anything leak?

Access control is missing almost everywhere: anyone can act as any customer, read any order, use the admin functions and dump the order table through the search route. A key named like a live payment key is in the code. These need fixing before anything else.

  • #1 Charged twice for one pair (closed: "could not reproduce by clicking once")
  • #2 Double charge again: clicked once, then reloaded while the page was loading

Why it keeps happening A purchase has no identity: each request is a new purchase, with no idempotency key sent to the provider and no rule that a customer has one order per product. The ticket was closed because a single click could not reproduce it, and nobody tested a double click or a reload during payment.

What catches the next one A unique rule on (customer, product) in the database, an idempotency key per purchase attempt passed to the provider, and the double-click acceptance test (AC-04) plus the race test with two clicks per buyer, run on every change.

Kind of test End-to-end tests in a browser, Load and race tests, Integration tests

Checked Run against this commit: AC-04 fails in all three runs (2 orders after a double-click) and the race test reports 957 buyers charged twice, so both tests catch it. Neither runs automatically yet.

Rule for AI agents Every purchase carries one idempotency key from the page to the provider; never create an order without it. AC-04 and the race test must pass.

More sold than in stock, and more than one pair per customer

Not caught automatically

Seen 2 times

  • #3 One person bought 3 pairs although the limit is one per customer
  • #4 Pilot stock was 20 pairs; 37 paid orders

Why it keeps happening The business rules live only as an if-statement in application code, followed by a separate write of a number read earlier; the database has no constraint, and the card is charged between the check and the write, which widens the gap. Nobody tested many buyers at once.

What catches the next one An atomic reservation (UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0), CHECK (stock >= 0) and a unique (customer, product) rule in the database, proven by the race test in CI.

Kind of test Load and race tests, Integration tests, Automatic scans

Checked The race test on this commit: 1,957 orders for 100 pairs (it catches it). The Semgrep rule stock-lost-update-sql also fired on app/server.mjs:111.

Rule for AI agents Stock and per-customer limits are enforced only by the database (atomic update, constraints); never check-then-write in code. The race test must pass.

Customers charged but no order recorded

Not caught automatically

Seen 2 times

  • #7 After a restart, two testers who had paid had no order
  • #10 Card charged, the page said sold out, and no order

Why it keeps happening The purchase charges the card before it records anything, keeps orders only in memory and deletes them at start-up, and has no "pending" state or reconciliation with the provider. Any interruption between charge and record (crash, deploy, error) loses the order while the money is taken.

What catches the next one A pending order written before the charge, a durable database with no destructive start-up, a settlement and reconciliation job that alerts on any difference, and an integration test that interrupts a purchase and restarts the app.

Kind of test Integration tests, Self-checks, Load and race tests

Checked No control exists. The reviewer's reproduction (evidence/probes-charged-no-order.txt) shows the gap and can become that test.

Rule for AI agents Never charge before a pending order is stored; never delete data at start-up; every provider charge must have an order (reconciliation must report zero differences).

The server trusts the browser: someone else's data, the price, admin functions

Partly caught automatically

Seen 3 times

  • #8 Changing the number in an order link showed another customer's name and address
  • #9 An order was paid at $0.01
  • #16 Anyone can open the sales stats page

Why it keeps happening There is no server-side authority: identity is an unsigned token the browser can write, the price is whatever the browser sends, and each route decides for itself whether to check anything, so some check nothing at all.

What catches the next one Signed sessions verified in one place for every route, a deny-by-default rule for admin routes, prices read from the database, and tests that call every route as nobody, as another customer and with a tampered price; the Semgrep rules unverified-token-decode, price-from-client and admin-route-inventory in CI.

Kind of test Integration tests, End-to-end tests in a browser, Automatic scans

Checked AC-03 and AC-06 fail on this commit (they catch the price and privacy problems); the three Semgrep rules fired on lines 46, 105, 132 and 139. No test calls the admin routes without credentials.

Rule for AI agents Every route checks a signed session on the server; prices and permissions come from the database, never from the request. AC-03, AC-06 and the admin-access test must pass.

Errors crash the site or show the code to visitors

Not caught automatically

Seen 3 times

  • #5 Site down for 10 minutes; last log line a SyntaxError from JSON.parse (closed: "restarted, working again")
  • #6 Site crashed again with the same error
  • #15 A failed purchase showed a long technical error with file names and line numbers

Why it keeps happening There is no single place that turns errors into safe answers: request bodies are parsed outside the error handling, so one bad request kills the process, and the error handler that does exist sends the raw stack to the visitor. The outage ticket was closed after a restart, without looking for the cause.

What catches the next one One error-handling layer (parse bodies and URLs inside it, answer 400 or a plain 500 with a request id), a supervisor that restarts the process, an integration test that sends malformed requests and checks the site still answers, and the Semgrep rules json-parse-in-stream-callback, url-parse-outside-try and stack-trace-to-client in CI.

Kind of test Integration tests, Automatic scans, Unit tests

Checked The three Semgrep rules fired on this commit (lines 38, 166, 174), so the scan catches it; the malformed-request test does not exist yet (evidence/probes-restarts.txt part A shows the crash).

Rule for AI agents All input parsing happens inside the error handler; visitors never see stack traces. The malformed-request test and the Semgrep rules must pass.

Slow pages and long waits under load or with a slow payment provider

Partly caught automatically

Seen 2 times

  • #11 Product page took 5 to 8 seconds with about 60 staff on it
  • #12 Buy button spun for about 30 seconds, then an error, while the provider was slow

Why it keeps happening Nothing was measured before the pilot: the product page makes one database query per review, nothing is cached, and neither the database pool nor the payment call has a time limit, so waiting is unbounded.

What catches the next one The staged load test and the slow-partner test from the owner's brief, run before every release with fixed budgets; time limits on every outside call; AC-08 in CI.

Kind of test Load and race tests, Integration tests

Checked The load test fails on this commit at 50% of the target and AC-08 fails in all three runs, so both catch it; neither runs automatically.

Rule for AI agents Every outside call has a time limit and every hot read is cached or a single query; the load test from peak-brief.json must stay within budget.

Sign-in box does not go away after signing in

Not caught automatically

Seen 2 times

  • #13 Sign-in box still showing after signing in (closed: "works for me")
  • #14 Same on an Android phone

Why it keeps happening The page hides elements with the hidden attribute, but the stylesheet's form { display: flex } overrides it, and no test checks that something disappears. The first ticket was closed as "works for me".

What catches the next one A browser test that checks the sign-in form is hidden after sign-in, and screenshot comparisons of the signed-in page on a computer and a phone.

Kind of test Visual tests, End-to-end tests in a browser

Checked No control: AC-02 passes while its own screenshot shows the problem (evidence/acceptance/AC-02-test-finished-1.png).

Rule for AI agents When the page hides something, a test checks it is hidden (toBeHidden()), on desktop and phone.

Product

A one-page web shop for a midnight sneaker drop: 100 pairs of limited-edition sneakers at $49.99, one pair per customer. Shoppers sign in with their email address, enter a shipping address and press Buy now; the server charges the card through a payment provider and confirms the order. About 3,000 visitors are expected in the first minute after an email announcement. Status: built and piloted with staff on 16 October 2026; not live. No review pack was handed in: the author's sections of this pack were filled in by the reviewer from the repository and are marked as such.

Users Public shoppers (consumers) on phones and computers, signing in with an email address; the shop team, who reset the sale and read the sales figures. Expected: about 3,000 visitors in the first minute after midnight. (Reviewer-built from the README and peak-brief.json.)

Out of scope

  • The payment-provider simulator and the database simulation (shared/fake-payment-provider.mjs, shared/db.mjs): infrastructure stand-ins, not code under review.
  • Choosing the real payment provider, email provider and hosting (not done yet; see decisions).

Risk tier 3 The app's own server charges cards through the payment provider's charge API, it opens with a rush (3,000 visitors in the first minute on limited stock), and it stores customers' email and home addresses High risk: the app takes payments itself, holds sensitive data, or launches with a big rush. Every Critical or High problem blocks launch, and backups, alerts and an on-call person must be shown.

users sign instores personal data (names, emails, addresses, messages, health, financial)takes payments, issues refunds or credits, or holds balancessells or allocates something limited (stock, seats, coupons, slots)has admin or staff functionsexpects a launch, promotion or other traffic spikeAI coding agents or assistants write or change the code

How to run it

Can a reviewer start work from the README alone?

For whoever runs the app: usually the developer.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22.13 or later (reviewed with 22.22.0)
  • For the tests: npm, and Chromium for Playwright 1.56.1

Commands

Set up
No packages for the app
cd acceptance && npm ci && npx playwright install chromium
Start
node run.mjs app   (PORT and PAYMENT_PORT change the ports)
Open
http://127.0.0.1:3000
Test
cd acceptance && npx playwright test --repeat-each=3   (APP_PORT / PAYMENT_PORT for other ports)
Reset test data
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/admin/reset -H "content-type: application/json" -d '{"stock":100}'   (not in the README; the route is open to anyone, see SEC-03)

Test copy (staging) None provided.

AdminNo admin accounts exist; the admin routes check nothing (see SEC-03)

Glossary

race test
Many simulated shoppers press Buy at the same instant, to see whether the shop sells more than it has or charges anyone twice.
load test
Simulated visitors arriving at a set rate, stepped up to and beyond the expected crowd, to measure how fast the site answers.
95th percentile
95% of requests were faster than this time.
idempotency key
A unique code sent with a payment so that if the same request arrives twice, the provider charges only once.
SQL injection
Typing database commands into a form or address so the server runs them.
token
The proof of sign-in the browser sends with each request. Here it is just the email address, so anyone can make one.
staging copy
A separate copy of the shop, set up like the real one, for testing without risk.
CI
Continuous integration: a service that runs the tests and checks automatically on every change.
rate limit
A cap on how many requests one person or address may make in a short time.
waiting room
A queue page that lets visitors into the sale a few at a time when too many arrive.
reconciliation
Comparing the payment provider's charges with the shop's orders and flagging any difference.
graceful shutdown
When the server is told to stop, it finishes the requests in progress before exiting.
health check
An address the hosting platform calls to see whether the app is running and can reach what it needs.
Semgrep
A tool that searches code for risky patterns.
Gitleaks
A tool that searches code and its history for passwords and keys.
k6
The tool used to run the load and race tests.
Lighthouse
A Google tool that measures how fast a page loads on a simulated phone.
axe
A tool that checks a page for accessibility problems.
SIGTERM
The signal a hosting platform sends to tell the app to stop, for example during a deploy.
CORS
A browser rule about which other websites may call the shop's server from a visitor's browser.
